doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: First hearing bebop and joining the Harold Fox big band
summary: A friend plays Charlie Parker Dial records; an anti-bebop bandleader dismisses the new style.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Tell us about the first time you heard bebop. And do you remember what your reaction was?

Yeah I remember the first time I heard it. It wasn’t on — was it on records or not? I think it was probably the same time — I was in high school, or I had just graduated from high school I think, or maybe during my last year of high school. I really was getting into it. And so there was a saxophone player who was a good friend of mine who was really a Lester Young fanatic. And then he heard Charlie Parker, you know and he was talking about Charlie Parker. He says, “Oh you’ve got to listen to this.” So I went over to his house and he had these old Dial 78s. And he played them for me, and I said wow, I hadn’t heard anything like that. So then I had a gig on weekends. I was working with this band that played just, they call it traditional swing now, you know, just straight ahead jazz. And nobody played bebop. They played good, the saxophone player was like Illinois Jacquet style, the saxophone player, like Texas Tenor style, which I still love today. But the bass player, who was the leader, was very anti bebop. He was really anti bebop. In fact he didn’t like the drummer, because the drummer had gotten into bebop drums, you know, like Max Roach and that. And he used to tell him, “Stop dropping those bombs.” That’s what he used to say, “Stop dropping those bombs.” So one night, two guys came by and wanted to sit in. One was an alto player and the other was a trumpet player. They were young too, they were around my age, maybe a couple of years older, I guess they were maybe about nineteen or twenty. And so the bass player let them sit in, and the saxophone player sounded wonderful. He was like imitating Charlie Parker. And the trumpet player was playing like Dizzy, like the trumpet player, and they started calling him “Little Diz.” And man, I heard this and I said wow, you know? And I loved it. And the bass player, oh he was furious. He said, “Man they’re playing that garbage.” He said, “Junior, don’t listen to that, that’ll never go anywhere. It will just phase itself out quick.” So he was saying this and it just went in one ear and out the other. But I got these guys’ phone numbers and I started hanging out with them. And that’s when I really got into it. So after this gig was over, I got another gig with a big band in Chicago, it was called Jimmy Dale, which was a pseudonym. There was a Jimmy Dale who was an arranger, but this was not the same Jimmy Dale. Jimmy Dale used to put out stock arrangements, but this was a different guy. This was a guy named Harold Fox who had Fox Brothers Tailors. He made uniforms for all the bands that were on the road. And the band was like a Who’s Who. The band was — well you know how they have the Monday night bands here like when Thad Jones and Mel Lewis used to play at the Vanguard every Monday night. Well that’s the kind of band we were. So Gene was in the band, Gene Ammons. Gene Ammons was in the band, Lee Konitz was in the band, he was from Chicago, Eugene Wright was the bass player, and all the guys were just fantastic players. And we did more rehearsing than playing but we just loved getting together every week just to rehearse. And we had a book that was out-a-sight. Because what Harold would do,
